subject: Biology
title: Your Microbial Self
description: A short lesson to help you apply Your Microbial Self.

hook.text: You carry about 38 trillion microbes—roughly as many as your own human cells.

buildup.text: These microbes live on your skin, in your gut, mouth, and nearly every surface of your body.

discovery.text: Together they weigh about 2 kilograms—as much as your brain.

twist.text: Your microbiome's genes outnumber your own genes by about 100 to 1.

climax.text: This microbial community helps digest food, train immunity, and even influence your mood.

punchline.text: You're as much microbe as you are human.

quiz.question: How many microbes does the average human body carry?

details.summary: The human body hosts approximately 38 trillion microbial cells, roughly matching the number of human cells. This personal microbiome weighing about 200 grams inhabits the gut, skin, mouth, and other surfaces, performing functions from digestion to immune training that we cannot live without.
details.whyItMatters: We are as much microbial as human. Our microbiome influences weight, mood, disease susceptibility, and drug metabolism. Understanding this intimate partnership is reshaping medicine from a focus on killing microbes to maintaining microbial balance.
takeaways: Your body contains roughly equal numbers of human and microbial cells
The gut microbiome alone contains 500 to 1,000 bacterial species
Each person's microbiome is unique, like a microbial fingerprint

faq.question: Are there really as many bacterial cells as human cells in your body?
faq.answer: Current estimates put the ratio at approximately 1 to 1, about 38 trillion bacteria to 30 trillion human cells. Earlier claims of 10 to 1 were overestimates. Despite similar numbers, bacterial cells are much smaller, making up only about 200 grams of body weight.

faq.question: Why is each person's microbiome unique?
faq.answer: Birth method, breastfeeding, diet, antibiotics, pets, environment, and genetics all shape your microbial community. Identical twins share more similar microbiomes than strangers, but significant differences exist even between twins. Your microbiome is as individual as a fingerprint.
